title: Exploring isovist fields: space and shape in architectural and urban morphology

findings.antecedent: minimum distance of isovist field (T-shape geometry)
findings.consequent: average distance of isovist field (T-shape geometry)
findings.mechanism: The minimum and average distances are both measures of how far one can see from a vantage point, and in the T-shape geometry, they show a moderate positive relationship.
findings.quote: plot of minimum distance in figure 3(c) which is correlated with the average distance at around 0.5.

findings.antecedent: maximum distance of isovist field (T-shape geometry)
findings.consequent: area and perimeter of isovist field (T-shape geometry)
findings.mechanism: High correlations between maximum distance, area, and perimeter suggest that 'how far' and 'how much' one can see are similar, implying a higher degree of compactness.
findings.quote: all correlations are greater than 0.84, indicating 'how far' and 'how much' one can see are similar

findings.mechanism: The compactness ratio effectively identifies areas within the interstices of the T-shape as being the most compact.
findings.quote: The ratio field {Γi} seems to be the better measure of compactness in that it picks up those areas above, below, and within the interstices of the T-shape as being the most compact.

findings.mechanism: The shape measure {Ψi} tends to disregard boundary effects and aligns more closely with the clustering measure.
findings.quote: the shape measure {Ψi} tends to ignore the influence of boundary effects and is much closer to the measure of clustering

findings.antecedent: shape index {Ψi} of isovist field (T-shape geometry)
findings.consequent: clustering index {γi} of isovist field (T-shape geometry)
findings.mechanism: A close spatial correspondence is observed between the shape index and clustering index, suggesting they might be similar measures of convexity.
findings.quote: A comparison of figure 3(h) with figure 5(a) in Turner et al (2001, page 110 of this issue) reveals a close spatial correspondence

findings.mechanism: The scatter plot of area against perimeter reveals at least two distinct types of isovists, indicating different spatial configurations.
findings.quote: area against perimeter... at least two types of isovist.

findings.mechanism: The scatter plot of area against the cluster ratio {Ψi} indicates at least two distinct types of isovists, reflecting variations in shape and visibility.
findings.quote: area against the shape index {Ψi}... at least two types of isovist.

findings.consequent: frequency distributions of average, minimum, and maximum distance
findings.mechanism: The simple T-shape geometry does not produce distinct types in distance distributions, showing only mild skews.
findings.quote: average, minimum, and maximum distance distributions do not reveal any distinct types. These show mild negative and positive skews

findings.consequent: frequency distributions of area and perimeter
findings.mechanism: The area and perimeter distributions are trimodal, indicating three distinct types of visual fields within the T-shape geometry.
findings.quote: area and perimeter distributions are examined, these distributions are trimodal with three distinct modal types.

findings.mechanism: The compactness ratio distribution for the T-shape exhibits greater normality with only a mild positive skew.
findings.quote: When we examine {Γi}, there is greater normality with only a mild positive skew.

findings.mechanism: The cluster ratio distribution shows two modes and a long right-hand tail, indicating a small number of very compact shapes and a larger number of less compact shapes.
findings.quote: For the ratio {Ψi}, two modes are apparent, together with a long right-hand tail giving a highly positive skew.

findings.antecedent: average distance, area, and perimeter of isovist fields (Manhattan grid geometry)
findings.mechanism: Strong correlations suggest that these basic measures of visibility are closely related in the Manhattan grid, indicating consistent spatial properties.
findings.quote: The strongest correlations exist between average distance, area, and perimeter with all correlations being greater than 0.89.

findings.antecedent: average distance of isovist field (Manhattan grid geometry)
findings.consequent: compactness ratio of isovist field (Manhattan grid geometry)
findings.mechanism: The compactness ratio is highly correlated with average distance, but the clustering index shows greater variability due to inner edge effects.
findings.quote: The compactness ratio is highly correlated with average distance but the clustering index shows much greater variation in being influenced by inner edge effects.

findings.mechanism: Two distinct types of elemental shapes (inner square spaces and spaces between block corners) are more clearly evident in perimeter measures than in area relationships.
findings.quote: These two types of elemental shape are more clearly evident in the perimeter measures than in any relationships involving area.

findings.antecedent: average distance of isovist field (Manhattan grid geometry)
findings.consequent: perimeter of isovist field (Manhattan grid geometry)
findings.mechanism: The scatter plot reveals two distinct sets of objects: inner square spaces between block edges and square spaces between block corners.
findings.quote: The scatter of average distances against perimeters shows two distinct sets of objects—inner square spaces between the edges of blocks and square spaces between the corners of blocks.

findings.consequent: frequency distributions of average distance, maximum distance, and area
findings.mechanism: These distributions are clearly bimodal, reflecting the two distinct types of spatial configurations in the Manhattan grid, while perimeter is trimodal.
findings.quote: Average distance, maximum distance, and area are clearly bimodal in contrast to perimeter which is trimodal.

findings.consequent: frequency distributions of compactness and clustering indices
findings.mechanism: Both compactness and clustering indices are bimodal, reflecting the two types of shapes present, with compactness positively skewed and clustering mildly negative.
findings.quote: The compactness and clustering indices are also bimodal, reflecting the two types of shape with the compactness distribution positively skewed, the clustering mildly negative

findings.mechanism: The regular, open nature of the Manhattan grid results in less compact and clustered isovists compared to the more enclosed T-shape.
findings.quote: the isovists associated with the Manhattan grid are much less compact and clustered than their T-shape equivalents.

findings.mechanism: The gallery's linear structure, defined by long axial lines, creates clear spatial correlations across the isovist fields.
findings.quote: There are clear spatial correlates between each of the fields based on the domination of a few long axial lines which define the overall linear structure of the gallery.

findings.antecedent: maximum distance, area, and perimeter of isovist fields (Tate Gallery)
findings.mechanism: These measures are highly correlated, indicating that 'how far' and 'how much' one can see are closely linked in the Tate Gallery's complex layout.
findings.quote: it is very marked for maximum distance, area, and perimeter which are all highly correlated.

findings.mechanism: The compactness index highlights smaller, squarer, and more remote rooms as the most compact spaces, reflecting typical vistas cutting through rooms.
findings.quote: the most compact spaces are the smaller, squarer, and more remote rooms in the gallery.

findings.antecedent: compactness index of isovist field (Tate Gallery)
findings.consequent: clustering index of isovist field (Tate Gallery)
findings.mechanism: A moderate correlation between clustering and compactness suggests a relationship between how enclosed a space feels and its visual connectivity.
findings.quote: The index of clustering also correlates with compactness at 0.662

findings.mechanism: All distributions are positively skewed, especially for maximum distance, area, and perimeter, with no bimodality, indicating a continuous range of visual experiences.
findings.quote: All the distributions are positively skewed, particularly the maximum distance, area, and perimeter distributions. None of the histograms shows any degree of bimodality

findings.mechanism: The Tate Gallery's complex layout results in a lower overall compactness compared to simpler geometries like the T-shape and Manhattan grid, but higher clustering than the Manhattan grid.
findings.quote: although the compactness index for the whole system is lower than in the first two examples, the cluster index is a lot higher than for the Manhattan grid

findings.antecedent: average distance and area of isovist fields (Regent Street)
findings.mechanism: A very high correlation indicates that in Regent Street, the average distance one can see is strongly linked to the total visible area, reflecting smooth spatial variation.
findings.quote: The maps of average distance and area are highly correlated at 0.942 and fairly smooth in their spatial variation.

findings.mechanism: The curve obstructs long vistas, reducing the maximum distance one can see.
findings.quote: the effect of the massive curve in Regent Street is evident in the way this interferes with vistas.

findings.antecedent: maximum distance of isovist field (Regent Street)
findings.mechanism: A strong correlation suggests that the extent of the farthest view is related to the visible perimeter, indicating consistent visual field properties.
findings.quote: quite highly correlated with perimeter at 0.784

findings.antecedent: area and perimeter of isovist fields (Regent Street)
findings.mechanism: Area and perimeter are highly correlated, similar to average distance and area, reflecting consistent visual field characteristics.
findings.quote: the area and perimeter maps are highly correlated with each other in the same manner as average distance and area.

findings.mechanism: Golden Square's central vantage point is the most compact, while tiny street indentations are more compact than long, narrow streets, reflecting varied spatial experiences.
findings.quote: The compactness index is dominated by Golden Square, whose central vantage point is the most compact of anywhere in the area; the tiny squares... are more compact than the long narrow streets

findings.mechanism: Long streets have low convexity, while squares (like Golden Square and Piccadilly Circus) have much greater convexity, indicating distinct visual fans and spatial experiences.
findings.quote: The index of clustering shows up these patterns quite clearly, with the long streets having low convexity values in contrast to squares which have much greater convexity in shape.

findings.consequent: frequency distributions of average distance, area, and perimeter
findings.mechanism: These distributions are clearly bimodal with mild positive skews, reflecting the distinct types of spaces (long streets vs. squares) in the morphology.
findings.quote: The distributions of average distance, area, and perimeter are clearly bimodal with mild positive skews

findings.mechanism: The farthest distance field is very positively skewed with a long right-hand tail, indicating a few very long streets that significantly extend visual reach.
findings.quote: The farthest distance field is very positively skewed with a long right-hand tail associated with the few very long streets within the morphology.

findings.mechanism: The compactness index is positively skewed, indicating a small number of very compact objects (squares) in the scene.
findings.quote: the compactness index is again positively skewed, reflecting the fact that there are only a small number of very compact objects in the scene.

findings.mechanism: The convexity index is much more normally distributed, suggesting a more uniform distribution of convex shapes.
findings.quote: The convexity index, however, is much more normally distributed.

findings.mechanism: The dominance of long streets in Regent Street's morphology leads to the lowest average compactness among all examples studied.
findings.quote: the compactness index is the lowest in all our examples to date, reflecting the domination of long streets.

findings.mechanism: Average distance is higher at street junctions and interstices due to more open space, reflecting the street-dominated morphology.
findings.quote: The average distance from each vantage point simply mirrors the fact that there is more space at junctions of streets and in the occasional interstices

findings.mechanism: The average distance field is the smoothest, being composed of averages, in contrast to the maximum distance field which is dominated by a few long streets.
findings.quote: this field is the smoothest of all, being composed of averages in contrast to the maximum distance which is dominated by four or five long streets.

findings.mechanism: Area and perimeter fields show largest values where streets enter squares, indicating clearer interaction between these spatial elements.
findings.quote: areas and perimeters where streets enter squares have the largest values.

findings.antecedent: average distance, area, and perimeter of isovist fields (Wolverhampton town center)
findings.mechanism: High correlations (greater than 0.75) indicate a strong relationship between these basic visibility measures, consistent with other examples.
findings.quote: The average distance, area, and perimeter fields are highly correlated with one another with correlations greater than 0.75 in every case

findings.mechanism: Inner parts of squares and some junctions exhibit highest compactness, while middle portions of long streets have the least, reflecting varied visual enclosure.
findings.quote: The inner parts of squares and some junctions have the highest compactness with the middle portions of long streets having the least.

findings.mechanism: Areas on the edges of streets show higher convexity than center lines, attributed to the relative irregularity of the town plan.
findings.quote: The convexity field shows that areas on the edges of streets have higher convexity than the center lines, this being a result of the relative irregularity of the town plan.

findings.mechanism: Unlike previous examples, the visual fields of Wolverhampton town center do not show distinct elements or clear groupings, appearing relatively uniform.
findings.quote: it is not possible to detect distinct elements in the visual fields of Wolverhampton town center. The street scenes appear to be relatively uniform.

findings.mechanism: All six plots are positively skewed but mildly so, with the convexity index being almost normally distributed, showing no bimodality or major deviations from normality.
findings.quote: there is no evidence whatsoever of any bimodality or other major deviations from normality. All six plots are positively skewed but only mildly so, with the exception of the convexity index which is almost normally distributed.

findings.mechanism: The morphology, dominated by long streets, results in the lowest average compactness among all examples studied.
findings.quote: Wolverhampton has the lowest average compactness of any of the examples we have dealt with, a fact that simply confirms a morphology dominated by long streets.

findings.antecedent: polygon with P vertices or edges and H holes
findings.consequent: minimum number of guards/isovists to cover the space
findings.mechanism: The Art Gallery Theorem states that at most P/3 guards (or (P+2H)/3 with holes) are sufficient to cover the space.
findings.quote: at most, P/3 guards or isovists are sufficient and sometimes necessary to cover the space; if the space has H holes, then (P+2H)/3 guards are required (O'Rourke, 1987).

findings.antecedent: Tate Gallery morphology (P=820 edges, H=33 holes)
findings.consequent: number of isovists required to cover the space using the algorithm
findings.mechanism: While the theoretical maximum is 296 isovists, the implemented algorithm covers the gallery with 84 isovists.
findings.quote: By using our algorithm, the gallery can in fact be covered by 84 isovists

findings.antecedent: total area seen along a path (Regent Street)
findings.consequent: average distance seen along the path (Regent Street)
findings.mechanism: Strong correlation indicates that changes in visible area are closely linked to changes in average visible distance, reflecting the spatial experience of moving through streets and squares.
findings.quote: Total area seen from this path is correlated very strongly with the average distance seen and these profiles... illustrate clearly the changes in space encountered

findings.mechanism: Narrow streets allow for long views, except where curves (like Regent Street from Piccadilly Circus) or edge effects obstruct vision.
findings.quote: the walk is dominated by narrow streets where the walker can see a long way, except when entering Regent Street from Piccadilly Circus where the curve obstructs vision

findings.antecedent: isovist fields in Piccadilly Circus (Regent Street)
findings.mechanism: Positions where long distances and large areas are visible provide a measure of spaciousness, contributing to a 'true' sensation of what a walker might feel.
findings.quote: where the walker can see long distances and large areas, thus providing a measure of spaciousness, a 'true' sensation of what a real walker might feel in this area.

findings.antecedent: major junctions along a path (Regent Street)
findings.mechanism: The perimeter measure dramatically increases at major junctions, reflecting the sudden expansion of the visual field.
findings.quote: This feature of the walk is also picked up from the perimeter measure which increases quite dramatically at major junctions.

findings.antecedent: changes in direction and area seen along a path (Regent Street)
findings.mechanism: The compactness index, which reflects how enclosed a walker feels, is highly sensitive to variations in both viewing direction and the visible area.
findings.quote: The index of compactness, however, which captures how enclosed the walker feels, is very sensitive to changes in both direction and the area seen

findings.mechanism: The clustering/convexity measure shows a more uniform trend but is 'noisy' due to local detail from pixelation, indicating less sensitivity to overall changes but high sensitivity to fine-grained features.
findings.quote: the clustering or convexity of spaces defining the walk is more uniform as a trend, yet much more 'noisy' as a profile in that this measure picks up all the local detail associated with the pixelation of the street map.

stimuli.description: Computational models of hypothetical and real-world architectural and urban geometries, represented as 2D grids of pixels.
Hypothetical T-shape geometry within a square grid (51x51 pixels).
Room plan of London's Tate Gallery (187x187 pixels).
Street plan of London's Regent Street and Piccadilly Circus area (215x215 pixels).
Street plan of Wolverhampton town center (187x187 pixels).

tables.description: Properties and basic field data for isovist fields across different applications (T-shape, Manhattan grid, Tate Gallery, Regent Street, Wolverhampton).
Properties and statistics (Mean, Standard deviation, Skewness) of the compactness coefficient {Γi} for various isovist fields and idealized geometries.
Properties and statistics (Mean, Standard deviation, Skewness) of the clustering/convexity coefficient {Ψi} for various isovist fields and idealized geometries.

limitations: The computational resolution (200x200 pixels) might be too coarse to pick up fine detail in city centers, potentially affecting substantive interpretations.
The analysis of the T-shape geometry introduced edge effects from the bounding box, which can distort results.
There is no formal demonstration that the index of shape {Ψi} and the index of clustering {γi} are similar, leaving this as a conjecture for future work.
A much wider range of morphological types is needed for a comprehensive classification and development of a robust theory of morphology.
Better measures of shape consistent with new ideas concerning convexity and isovist geometry are still needed.
A specific statistical theory needs to be developed to fully understand the interplay of geometry and the local dynamics of visual movement.
The measures are not scale invariant, and visual experiences will vary across scale; local detail at very fine levels cannot yet be simulated.
Larger systems are required to minimize boundary effects, as seen in the Regent Street example where lines of sight outside the system likely produced significant distortions.
There is a need for further research into partition problems to simplify space into distinct subspaces or covers.
